Opera ad Extra
ŏp´ĕ-ră ad eks´tră
n. phrase (Latin: the Trinity's works toward the creature, which are undivided)
Latin opera, works, + ad extra, toward what is outside. The schools distinguished these from opera ad intra, the personal works that stay within the Godhead (generation, spiration). Outward, the three Persons work one work. Inward, the relations of origin remain distinct.

Biblical Definition

Opera ad extra are the works God does toward the world, and they are not split among the Persons as if creation were the Father's hobby and redemption the Son's. “In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth” (Gen 1:1), and the Spirit was there: “And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters” (Gen 1:2), and the Word was there: “All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made” (John 1:3). Paul will not let the church assign the works to separate gods: “But to us there is but one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, and we by him” (1Co 8:6). The same undivided work is in the raising: “But if the Spirit of him that raised up Jesus from the dead dwell in you, he that raised up Christ from the dead shall also quicken your mortal bodies by his Spirit that dwelleth in you” (Rom 8:11). One God. Three Persons. One work outward.

Origin & Era

Webster (1828) has no entry for the Latin phrase. Opera ad extra names the Trinity's outward works, which are undivided, as distinct from the inward personal properties.

expand to see more

OPERA AD EXTRA, Latin, works toward the outside. Scholastic Trinitarian phrase, not an 1828 English headword.

Creation, providence, incarnation, redemption, judgment: one work of the one God.

The Persons are not three agents splitting a job. Appropriations name how Scripture often speaks; they do not divide the essence.

Paired with opera ad intra: generation and spiration remain personal and inward.

Key Scripture

Gen 1:1 — "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth."

Gen 1:2 — "And the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters."

John 1:3 — "All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made."

1Co 8:6 — "But to us there is but one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, and we by him."

Rom 8:11 — "But if the Spirit of him that raised up Jesus from the dead dwell in you, he that raised up Christ from the dead shall also quicken your mortal bodies by his Spirit that dwelleth in you."

Modern Corruption

The outward works are either split into three jobs or collapsed so that the Persons are only masks, and Scripture will have neither.

expand to see more

A crude tritheism assigns creation to the Father, the cross to the Son, and Pentecost to the Spirit, as if the Godhead were a committee. Genesis 1 will not start that way, and John 1 will not let the Word be a subcontractor. All things were made by Him. First Corinthians 8:6 holds of whom and by whom in one confession, not two deities.

The modalist opposite hears undivided and concludes the Persons are costumes. Romans 8:11 names the Father who raised, the Son who was raised, and the Spirit who dwells and quickens, without splitting the work or erasing the names. Undivided is not unnamed.

Appropriations are a help when they stay humble. We say the Father creates, the Son redeems, the Spirit sanctifies, because Scripture often talks that way. We do not then write a fourth god called the Committee. The dictionary's Trinity is the one who made the world and raised the Son by the Spirit, and still is Father, Son, and Holy Ghost.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin opera ad extra; Hebrew bara (H1254), create; Greek ginomai (G1096) in John 1:3, were made.

Latin opera ad extra — outward works of the Trinity; undivided.

Hebrew bara (H1254) — create; Genesis 1:1, God created.

Greek egeneto (G1096) — were made; John 1:3, all things by the Word.

Usage

"“The Spirit of God moved” — already in the second verse."

"“All things were made by him” — the Word is not a subcontractor."

"“Of whom … by whom” — one confession, not two gods."
